Those efforts include reducing personal taxes, doubling infrastructure spending, injecting liquidity into financial markets and securing pension plans.

Although he did not specify what those legal means might entail, his opponents predicted that he would attempt to dissolve Parliament and quickly voiced their opposition.

The Liberal Party, which lost seats in the October election, and the leftist New Democratic Party announced plans earlier this week to form a governing coalition with the support of the Bloc Quebecois, which advocates independence for French-speaking Quebec.

(CNN) — In a nationally broadcast speech Wednesday focused on the economy, Prime Minister Stephen Harper sought Canadians’ backing and promised to use every available option to prevent opposition parties from proceeding with Monday’s planned no-confidence vote and replacing his administration with a coalition.

Harper accused the coalition’s leaders of “betrayal” because their proposed government would depend on support from Quebec separatists.

The prime minister said the opposition was attempting to reverse the outcome of the election only seven weeks after Canadians had voted—and before his government had even presented its budget. Harper’s Conservative Party increased its strength, though it remained a minority government, in the October 14 federal election.

Amid global instability, Harper argued, the federal government could not share power with a separatist party. He said Canada’s leadership must be unambiguous in its commitment to national unity.

Describing the situation as a crucial point in Canadian history, Harper outlined measures his government was taking in response to the economic downturn. Those steps included reducing personal taxes, doubling infrastructure expenditures, supplying liquidity to financial markets and safeguarding pension plans.

iReport.com: Anger growing in Canada.

Harper pledged that his government would employ every lawful tool available to defend Canadian democracy, the economy and the country itself. He did not explain which legal actions he was considering, but opposition leaders said they expected him to seek the dissolution of Parliament and immediately denounced that possibility.

Earlier in the week, the Liberal Party—which lost seats in October—and the left-leaning New Democratic Party announced an agreement to establish a coalition government. The arrangement would rely on backing from the Bloc Québécois, a party that advocates independence for predominantly French-speaking Quebec.

Liberal leader Stéphane Dion responded in his own televised statement after Harper’s address, demanding that the confidence vote go ahead. Dion said he had urged Governor General Michaëlle Jean, Canada’s acting head of state and the official responsible for calling either a new election or a confidence vote, to reject any attempt by Harper to suspend Parliament unless he first proved that he retained the confidence of the House of Commons.

Dion said Canada was already feeling the effects of the worldwide economic crisis and needed an immediate response. He accused Harper of refusing to introduce economic-stimulus measures and said the Conservatives no longer had the support of most members of the Commons. As a result, Dion argued, they no longer had the authority to remain in government.

Dion said he and New Democratic Party leader Jack Layton had agreed to create a coalition administration to confront the economic emergency. He added that the Green Party also supported the proposal.

Coalition governments, Dion said, are common in many countries and can function effectively. He accused Harper of prolonging the crisis by trying to avoid a straightforward vote, suspend Parliament and preserve the uncertainty. The coalition, he said, was offering a preferable alternative: resolve the matter immediately and begin addressing Canadians’ concerns. Dion insisted that Monday’s scheduled vote should proceed.

In a separate televised statement, Layton characterized Harper’s remarks as a partisan assault. He said the Conservative proposal would neither generate employment nor protect pensions. According to Layton, Harper appeared more concerned about preserving his own position than protecting Canadians’ jobs, which Layton called plainly wrong.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about Stephen Harper’s televised appeal during Canada’s 2008 parliamentary crisis and the opposition coalition’s response.
counterfactuals.output:
**Harper appeals to Canadians as opposition coalition presses bid to take power**

**OTTAWA, Ontario (CNN)** — Prime Minister Stephen Harper took to Canadian television Wednesday night to defend his minority Conservative government, warning that an opposition coalition seeking to replace it would overturn the results of the recent federal election and depend on support from Quebec separatists.

The December 3, 2008, address came amid one of Canada’s most serious parliamentary crises in decades. The Liberal Party and New Democratic Party had signed an agreement to form a coalition government, backed through a separate arrangement with the Bloc Québécois. Together, the parties said they had enough votes to defeat Harper’s government in the House of Commons.

“Canada’s government should be decided by Canadians, not backroom deals,” Harper said, portraying the coalition as an attempt to seize power weeks after voters returned the Conservatives with a strengthened—but still minority—mandate.

The opposition rejected that argument, saying Canada’s parliamentary system requires a government to maintain the confidence of the elected House, not merely win the most seats in an election.

Liberal leader Stéphane Dion responded in a televised statement, saying the coalition offered a stable alternative and would act more aggressively to protect Canadians from the global economic downturn. Dion accused Harper of provoking the crisis through partisan measures and an economic update that offered little immediate stimulus.

The coalition proposed that Dion serve as prime minister until the Liberals selected a permanent leader. It also promised an economic stimulus package and said the Bloc would support the government on confidence votes for 18 months without joining the Cabinet.

Dion’s response, however, was marred by technical problems. The recording arrived late to television networks and was criticized for poor video quality, undercutting the opposition’s effort to match Harper’s polished address.

The dispute centered on sharply different interpretations of democratic legitimacy. Harper insisted the coalition lacked a mandate and highlighted its reliance on the Bloc, while coalition leaders said replacing a government through a confidence vote was constitutional and consistent with parliamentary tradition.

The next day, Governor General Michaëlle Jean granted Harper’s request to suspend, or prorogue, Parliament until January 2009, temporarily preventing the confidence vote and giving the Conservatives time to prepare a budget aimed at retaining power.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the December 2008 Canadian political showdown involving Prime Minister Stephen Harper, Stéphane Dion, Jack Layton, and the Bloc Québécois, including key quotes from their televised addresses.
counterfactuals.output:
### What happened

After Stephen Harper’s Conservatives were re-elected with a minority government in October 2008, their November 27 fiscal update offered little immediate economic stimulus during the global financial crisis. It also proposed ending the public subsidy paid to political parties and temporarily restricting federal public servants’ right to strike. The opposition saw the measures as both inadequate and partisan.

Liberal leader **Stéphane Dion** and NDP leader **Jack Layton** therefore negotiated a formal coalition. Dion would become prime minister, with Liberals and New Democrats sharing cabinet posts. The **Bloc Québécois**, led by Gilles Duceppe, would not join the government but promised to support it on confidence votes for 18 months. Together, the three opposition parties held a Commons majority and planned to defeat Harper’s government.

Harper withdrew some contentious proposals but argued that replacing his government so soon after an election—especially with Bloc support—would be illegitimate. Constitutionally, however, a coalition commanding the confidence of the House could potentially govern without another election.

### The televised addresses, December 3

Harper addressed the country first. He portrayed the coalition as an attempt to reverse the election result through a deal with separatists:

> “The opposition is attempting to overturn the results of the last election without seeking your consent.”

He continued:

> “The opposition has every right to defeat the government, but Stéphane Dion does not have the right to take power without an election.”

And concluded the central argument:

> “Canada’s government should be decided by Canadians, not backroom deals. It should be your choice, not theirs.”

Harper’s description was politically powerful but constitutionally disputed: Canadians elect MPs, and a government remains in office only while it retains the confidence of the House of Commons.

Dion’s reply argued that Harper had lost that confidence and had failed to respond adequately to the recession:

> “The current government has lost the confidence of the House of Commons and indeed of the majority of Canadian voters.”

He presented the coalition as a legitimate and responsible alternative:

> “The opposition parties have acted responsibly and put aside their differences to offer a viable alternative government.”

Dion also emphasized economic action:

> “We offer a clear choice: a government that will provide Canadians with hope and a plan for the economy, instead of a government that has lost the confidence of the House.”

His address was badly damaged by presentation problems: the recording reached television networks late and was of noticeably poor video quality, reinforcing doubts about Dion’s political effectiveness.

### Layton and the Bloc

Layton vigorously defended the proposed coalition, saying at its public unveiling:

> “This is a good day for Canada.”

He argued that the opposition was responding to Harper’s failure to address job losses and the economic downturn, and that parliamentary cooperation—not another election—was the responsible course.

The Bloc’s role was crucial but limited. It would support the coalition on confidence matters while taking no cabinet seats. Harper repeatedly called the arrangement a coalition “with the separatists,” while Dion and Layton stressed that it was a Liberal–NDP government supported through a written parliamentary agreement with the Bloc.

### How it ended

On December 4, Harper asked Governor General **Michaëlle Jean** to prorogue, or suspend, Parliament before the scheduled confidence vote. She agreed, shutting Parliament until late January 2009. During the pause, the coalition lost momentum, Dion was replaced as Liberal leader by **Michael Ignatieff**, and the Liberals ultimately allowed Harper’s January budget to pass after securing amendments.

The showdown therefore ended without either a confidence vote or a coalition government, but it became a major Canadian constitutional and political controversy over parliamentary confidence, coalition legitimacy, the governor general’s discretion, and prime-ministerial use of prorogation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed breaking-news article explaining Harper’s effort to stop a no-confidence vote and prevent a Liberal–NDP coalition from replacing his Conservative minority government.
counterfactuals.output:
# Harper Wins Parliamentary Suspension, Delaying Vote That Could Topple Conservative Government

**OTTAWA — Dec. 4, 2008** — Prime Minister Stephen Harper has persuaded Governor General Michaëlle Jean to suspend Parliament, temporarily blocking a no-confidence vote that could have brought down his minority Conservative government and allowed a Liberal–New Democratic coalition to take power.

Jean approved Harper’s request Thursday after an extraordinary two-hour meeting at Rideau Hall. Parliament will be prorogued until Jan. 26, with the government expected to present a federal budget the following day.

The decision gives Harper nearly two months to regain political support, weaken the opposition alliance and prepare an economic plan capable of surviving a confidence vote. It also prevents the House of Commons from voting Monday on a Liberal motion declaring that the Conservatives have lost the confidence of Parliament.

Harper emerged from the meeting saying the government would use the suspension to develop a budget addressing the global economic crisis.

“The government will use this time to continue consulting with Canadians,” Harper said, promising measures to protect the economy. But opposition leaders accused him of shutting down Parliament simply to avoid certain defeat.

## Coalition was poised to replace Conservatives

The Liberals and NDP announced this week that they had formed a proposed coalition led by Liberal Leader Stéphane Dion. Under a written agreement, the two parties planned to govern together for at least 18 months, with the Bloc Québécois pledging to support the coalition on confidence matters during that period.

The Liberals would have held most cabinet positions, while the NDP would have entered the federal cabinet for the first time. Dion, who was already preparing to step down as Liberal leader after his party’s weak election performance, would have served as prime minister until the Liberals selected his successor.

Together, the Liberals and NDP hold 114 seats in the 308-seat Commons. Their agreement with the 49-member Bloc would have given them enough votes to defeat the Conservatives, who won 143 seats in the Oct. 14 election but remained short of a majority.

If Harper had lost the planned confidence vote, he would have been required either to resign or ask for another election. Because Canadians had voted less than two months earlier, Jean could instead have invited Dion to demonstrate that the coalition commanded the confidence of the House.

That constitutional possibility placed the governor general at the center of the crisis. As the Crown’s representative, Jean had to decide whether to accept Harper’s advice to prorogue Parliament even though his government faced an imminent confidence test.

She agreed, though the details of any conditions attached to the decision were not made public.

## Fiscal update ignited the confrontation

The crisis began after Finance Minister Jim Flaherty presented an economic and fiscal statement on Nov. 27.

Instead of unveiling a major stimulus package in response to the rapidly worsening global downturn, the Conservatives proposed measures that infuriated the opposition. The update included a plan to eliminate the public subsidy paid to political parties according to the number of votes they received, temporarily restrict the right of federal public employees to strike and limit their ability to pursue pay-equity complaints.

The proposed end to public financing threatened the opposition parties far more severely than the Conservatives, who have a stronger private fundraising operation. Opposition leaders portrayed the measure as an attempt to use the financial crisis to cripple political rivals.

The government soon retreated. It withdrew the party-financing proposal, backed away from some labor provisions and promised an early budget containing economic measures. But by then the Liberals, NDP and Bloc had reached an agreement to defeat Harper.

The Conservatives argued that the coalition was an illegitimate attempt to overturn the election result. Harper focused particular criticism on the coalition’s reliance on the Bloc, a party committed to Quebec sovereignty.

The opposition countered that Canada’s parliamentary system does not directly elect a prime minister or government. A ministry remains in office only while it retains the confidence of the House of Commons, they said, and parties controlling a majority of seats are constitutionally entitled to propose an alternative government.

The coalition would not have included Bloc cabinet ministers. The Bloc’s role would have been to provide outside support on confidence votes.

## Competing appeals to Canadians

Harper addressed the country on television Wednesday night, warning that the opposition arrangement would hand influence to separatists during a period of economic instability.

“At a time of global economic instability, Canada’s government must stand unequivocally for keeping the country together,” he said.

Dion responded on behalf of the coalition, accusing Harper of refusing to cooperate with other parties and failing to offer a serious response to the economic crisis. Technical and delivery problems delayed the broadcast of Dion’s recorded statement on some networks, weakening the opposition’s effort to counter Harper’s message.

The political battle now moves outside the Commons. Conservative MPs and cabinet ministers are expected to campaign aggressively during the suspension, seeking public opposition to the coalition and pressuring Liberal and NDP members to abandon it.

The government will also prepare a budget designed to survive when Parliament returns. Tax cuts, infrastructure spending, aid for struggling industries and other stimulus measures could make it politically difficult for some opposition MPs to vote the Conservatives out.

## Coalition faces its own strains

The delay creates significant risks for the opposition alliance.

Dion’s authority remains fragile after the Liberals won only 77 seats in October, one of the party’s worst results. He announced after the election that he would resign once a successor was chosen, and prominent Liberals Michael Ignatieff, Bob Rae and Dominic LeBlanc entered the leadership race.

Prorogation gives the Liberals time to replace Dion before Parliament returns. It also gives coalition critics within the party an opportunity to argue that the agreement should be reconsidered, especially if the Conservatives produce a popular budget.

NDP Leader Jack Layton has defended the coalition as a stable alternative focused on economic stimulus, job protection and support for vulnerable Canadians. Bloc Leader Gilles Duceppe has said his party’s support is based on obtaining action for Quebec, while insisting the Bloc would not formally join the government.

The coalition agreement called for a multibillion-dollar stimulus program, assistance for the automobile and forestry industries, investments in housing and infrastructure, and measures to protect pensions and employment.

## Harper survives, but only temporarily

Prorogation ends the current parliamentary session and halts all Commons business. It does not dissolve Parliament or trigger an election, and Harper remains prime minister with his cabinet in place.

But the move has postponed rather than eliminated the confidence question.

When Parliament returns, the government must present a new Speech from the Throne and budget. The budget will be a confidence matter. If the three opposition parties remain united and vote against it, the Conservatives could still fall.

Harper’s decision is therefore an effort to change the political conditions surrounding the vote, not to cancel the opposition’s ability to hold one indefinitely.

The confrontation is one of the sharpest tests of Canada’s parliamentary conventions in decades. It has opened a national debate over the powers of a minority government, the legitimacy of coalition rule and the governor general’s responsibility when a prime minister seeks to suspend Parliament while facing defeat.

For now, Harper has secured the time he wanted. Whether he can use it to save his government will be decided when MPs return in January.

### Canada’s political crisis moves to prime time

Amid the worsening global financial crisis, Prime Minister Stephen Harper, Liberal leader Stéphane Dion and NDP leader Jack Layton delivered competing televised messages over the future of the Conservative government.

Harper argued that the opposition was attempting to overturn the result of the October 2008 election without public consent. He condemned the proposed Liberal–NDP coalition because it would depend on promised support from the separatist Bloc Québécois. Harper said his government should be allowed to continue addressing the economy and sought Governor General Michaëlle Jean’s approval to prorogue—temporarily suspend—Parliament.

Prorogation would prevent a confidence vote scheduled for December 8. The Conservatives were expected to lose that vote after their fiscal update, which offered no major immediate stimulus and included contentious measures such as eliminating public subsidies for political parties. Defeat would normally require Harper either to resign or request another election.

Dion countered that the coalition was a lawful constitutional alternative, not an attack on democracy. He accused Harper of failing to respond adequately to the recession and of creating an avoidable parliamentary crisis. Under the coalition agreement, Dion would become prime minister of a Liberal–NDP government, with a cabinet divided between the two parties, until the Liberals selected a permanent leader. The Bloc would not join the cabinet but promised to support the coalition on confidence matters for 18 months.

Layton likewise presented the coalition as a stable, cooperative response to extraordinary economic conditions. He said Harper had placed partisan tactics and ideology ahead of jobs, pensions and economic stimulus, and argued that opposition parties representing a majority of elected MPs had both the right and the responsibility to form a government.

The central constitutional question was therefore whether Jean should grant Harper’s request to suspend Parliament or allow the confidence vote to proceed. Jean ultimately approved prorogation on December 4, postponing Parliament until January 26, 2009, and temporarily averting the government’s defeat.
